LEARNING PATH LESSON · GARDEN FRIENDS · AGES 2 YEARS

Deer — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson brings the quiet bigness of the deer indoors: slow tiptoes, listening ears and a first understanding that the biggest garden neighbours need the biggest distance.

What is this?

A deer is a large, gentle animal with long legs, big ears and soft fur that lives in woods and fields. Deer hear everything and move away fast and quietly.

What does it mean?

The deer stretches a toddler’s sense of scale — this neighbour is taller than you and still shy. Meeting bigness that needs space (not hugging) is an early lesson in how wild things stay well.

What does the child need to know?

Deer have big listening ears and long quiet legs. They are large wild animals: gentle to look at, never to approach. We watch from far away — through a window or from the path — and we speak in whispers.

Why this matters

Distance is a hard idea for toddlers, who show love by reaching. The deer card gives distance a positive shape: the farther away you are, the longer the deer stays — watching becomes a game of patience with a giant prize.

What it teaches

Whisper-level quiet, listening attention (what did we hear?), scale words (big, tall, huge), self-restraint with a visible reward, and the idea that size and wildness travel together.

Words to learn

deertallearsquietwoodsfar

Say this to your child

“"A deer! So tall, so quiet. Deer have big ears that turn and listen — can you make deer ears? They live in the woods and they move away softly. When we see a deer, we stay far away and whisper — that is how we say we love you to a deer."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card, say deer, and hold a hand high above your head — bigger than you, bigger than me — so the size arrives before the details.
  2. Make deer ears with your hands and swivel them slowly: deer listen all the time, and so will we for this game.
  3. Tiptoe across the room, freeze at every creak, and listen — the deer walk is tiptoe plus stop plus listen, repeated.
  4. Explain the distance rule in toddler terms: deer stay happy when we stay far; if we tiptoe closer, they vanish — so the game is to be the stillness they trust.
  5. End by looking out of a window or across a field together and counting what a deer might hear from there — a bird, a car, your whisper.

Look closer at the picture

Say deer and hold a hand high — taller than you, taller than me. Make swivelling ear-hands together, ask what the deer is doing on the card, then drop to a whisper: deer talk is quiet talk.

Ask your child

"Is the deer big or little?" "What are its ears doing?" "Show me the deer tiptoe." "Do we walk close to the deer, or stay far away?" — answered with ear-hands, a tiptoe and a stretched-out "faaar".

What your child can say or do

"Deer! Big one!" Expect ear-hands at bedtime, deer declared at the far end of parks, and sudden freezing mid-walk — ears up, listening. The whisper may spread to libraries and churches, courtesy of the deer.

Out in the real world

Deer appear at forest edges, parklands and safari-park windows, often at dawn or dusk. Each tall, quiet sighting is a rerun: freeze, whisper, count the seconds it stays — distance paying its dividend.

Try it together

Listening walk: indoors or out, tiptoe together and stop every few steps to name one sound you can both hear. Deer ears swivelling, toddler listening — attention training with antler-level dignity.

Understanding check

At the next deer-in-a-book moment, watch the volume: if your toddler drops to a whisper and stays planted, the distance rule has become instinct — the lesson is complete.

Parent tips

Let the deer own the vocabulary of quiet: "deer feet" for tiptoeing past a sleeping baby is a household trick with a long shelf life. If a safari park is ever nearby, the window view is the field trip.

Staying safe

Deer are large wild animals — never approach, feed or chase one, however calm it looks; a startled deer is powerful and unpredictable. Keep toddlers inside fences and in hands at safari parks and forest edges.

This lesson pairs with the Deer flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Garden Friends (School Garden).
